title: UTF-8, a transformation format of ISO 10646
summary: Specifies UTF-8, an encoding of the ISO 10646 / Unicode character set that preserves the US-ASCII range and works well with file systems, parsers and software that expect ASCII. It was designed for compatibility with applications not built for wider characters. It obsoletes RFC 2279 and is an Internet Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: UTF-8 is a way to store every character of the Unicode character set as bytes. It keeps plain English letters exactly as they were, so old programs that expect ASCII keep working, while rarer characters take two, three or four bytes each.

subtitle: How every Unicode character becomes one to four bytes, with plain ASCII left exactly as it was.

tldr.problem: The standard encodings of the Universal Character Set used units larger than one octet, which made them hard to use in applications and protocols that assume 7 or 8 bit characters.
tldr.mechanism: UTF-8 writes each character number as a sequence of 1 to 4 octets, where the first octet tells how long the sequence is. US-ASCII characters keep their normal one-octet values.
tldr.outcome: An Internet Standard that obsoletes RFC 2279. Software must reject invalid sequences, because decoding them can be a security hole.

today: RFC 3629 is an Internet Standard (STD 63) and the RFC text lists no later RFC that obsoletes it. It obsoletes RFC 2279 and remains the IETF specification of UTF-8.

sections.title: Why UTF-8 Exists
sections.content:
ISO/IEC 10646 defines the Universal Character Set (UCS), which covers most of the world's writing systems. The Unicode standard defines the same set of characters. Both define several encoding forms: UTF-8, UCS-2, UTF-16, UCS-4 and UTF-32.

All of them except UTF-8 use an encoding unit larger than one octet. That makes them hard to use in applications and protocols that assume 8 or even 7 bit characters. UTF-8 has a one-octet encoding unit and keeps the full US-ASCII range: an ASCII character is one octet with its normal ASCII value, and an octet with such a value can only mean that ASCII character.

The RFC lists further properties. The first octet of a multi-octet sequence says how many octets follow. The octet values C0, C1 and F5 to FF never appear. Character boundaries are easy to find from anywhere in a stream, and sorting UTF-8 strings byte by byte gives the same order as sorting by character number.

UTF-8 was devised in September 1992 by Ken Thompson, guided by design criteria from Rob Pike, for use in the Plan9 operating system. It was stewarded through standardization by the X/Open Joint Internationalization Group and carried the names FSS-UTF, UTF-2 and finally UTF-8.
sections.plainLanguage: UTF-8 exists because older ways of storing the full Unicode character set broke programs that expect plain ASCII bytes. UTF-8 keeps every ASCII byte unchanged, so those programs still work, and uses longer codes only for other characters.

sections.title: How Characters Become Octets
sections.content:
UTF-8 encodes characters in the range U+0000 to U+10FFFF using sequences of 1 to 4 octets. A single-octet sequence starts with a 0 bit and carries 7 bits of the character number. In a sequence of n octets (n greater than 1), the initial octet has the n higher-order bits set to 1 followed by a bit set to 0. Every following octet starts with the bits 10 and carries 6 bits of the character number.

To encode, pick the row of the table that fits the character number, prepare the high-order bits of each octet, then fill the marked bits from the character number, starting with its lowest-order bit in the last octet of the sequence. The rows of the table are mutually exclusive, so there is only one valid way to encode a character.

Character numbers from U+D800 to U+DFFF are reserved for UTF-16 surrogate pairs and must not be encoded. When converting from UTF-16 data, you must first decode the UTF-16 data to character numbers and then encode those. This differs from CESU-8, which encodes the 16-bit UTF-16 values and is not meant for use on the Internet.

Decoding builds a binary number of up to 21 bits from the marked bits of the sequence. Implementations MUST protect against decoding invalid sequences. For example, a naive decoder might turn the overlong sequence C0 80 into U+0000, or a pair of surrogate-like sequences into U+233B4.
sections.plainLanguage: Each character becomes one to four bytes. The first byte of a multi-byte sequence says how many bytes belong to that character, and every later byte in the sequence starts with the bits 10. Plain ASCII characters stay single bytes with their usual values.

sections.title: The ABNF Syntax of UTF-8
sections.content:
For implementors who use ABNF (Augmented BNF for Syntax Specifications), the RFC gives a grammar for valid UTF-8. An octet sequence is valid UTF-8 only if it matches the grammar. The grammar spells out the ranges the encoding rules imply: a one-octet character is %x00-7F, a two-octet character starts with a byte from C2 to DF, and every continuation byte (UTF8-tail) is in the range 80 to BF. Three- and four-octet forms are spelled out the same way, and the ranges exclude the overlong forms and the surrogate range.

The RFC adds a caution: the authoritative definition of UTF-8 is in the Unicode standard, and this grammar is believed to describe the same thing but does not claim to be authoritative. Implementors are urged to rely on the Unicode standard rather than on the ABNF.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a strict grammar of which byte patterns are valid UTF-8. Anything that does not match the grammar is not real UTF-8. The Unicode standard, not this grammar, is the authoritative definition.

sections.title: The Byte Order Mark
sections.content:
The character U+FEFF is formally "ZERO WIDTH NO-BREAK SPACE", but it is also informally called the byte order mark (BOM). It can be placed at the start of a stream as a signature that the stream holds characters in a Unicode encoding. In encodings with a multi-octet unit the initial character also reveals the order of the octets. UTF-8 has a single-octet encoding unit, so that function is useless and the BOM always appears as the octets EF BB BF.

A U+FEFF character at any position other than the start of a stream MUST be treated as a zero-width no-break space, not as a signature. Stripping an initial signature is RECOMMENDED only when really necessary, because it can upset an external process that relies on the presence of all characters, such as a digital signature or a character count.

The RFC gives protocol designers advice by case. A protocol SHOULD forbid the signature for elements that are always UTF-8, and for elements that carry their own encoding label and can be expected to use it properly. It SHOULD NOT forbid it where there is no encoding label or a ban could not be enforced, such as MIME entities obtained from file systems, FTP or HTTP.

Unicode 3.2 adds U+2060 "WORD JOINER", which has the same meaning as U+FEFF except for the signature function. Following the recommendation to use U+2060 for word-joining makes it all but certain that an initial U+FEFF is a signature.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes a file begins with an invisible marker character that says this is Unicode text. UTF-8 files do not need it, because the bytes already reveal the encoding, but some files carry it, so programs should be ready to see it and only remove it when they must.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC encodes four sequences by hand. The character sequence U+0041 U+2262 U+0391 U+002E (an A, a not-identical-to sign, a Greek alpha and a full stop) becomes 41 E2 89 A2 CE 91 2E.

The Korean word U+D55C U+AD6D U+C5B4, meaning the Korean language, becomes ED 95 9C EA B5 AD EC 96 B4. The Japanese word U+65E5 U+672C U+8A9E, meaning the Japanese language, becomes E6 97 A5 E6 9C AC E8 AA 9E.

The character U+233B4, a Chinese character meaning stump of tree, prepended with a UTF-8 byte order mark, becomes EF BB BF F0 A3 8E B4. The first three octets are the BOM and the last four are the character itself.
sections.plainLanguage: Plain letters take one byte, Greek and Korean and Japanese characters take three, and rare characters take four. The examples in the RFC show real words turned into their exact byte values.

sections.title: The MIME Charset Label
sections.content:
This memo is the basis for registering the MIME charset parameter value UTF-8. The label covers text in the ISO/IEC 10646 repertoire, including amendments at least up to amendment 5 of the 1993 edition, and is suitable for the text top-level MIME type.

The label deliberately carries no version number. A version label would risk an older application failing to recognize a newer label, when a generic label lets it process the data mostly correctly. The one incompatible change so far, the 1996 move and expansion of the Korean Hangul block nicknamed the "Korean mess", is judged harmless because there were no significant amounts of data using the old layout. The IANA charset entry for UTF-8 was updated to point to this memo.

The memo also explains why incompatible changes were ruled out: the relevant committees pledged to never again make such a change, and a version-independent label is warranted as long as the standards evolve compatibly.
sections.plainLanguage: The name tag UTF-8 has no version number on purpose. Older programs still recognize the tag when the character set grows, instead of rejecting a new version label they have never seen.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The main risk is how software handles illegal byte sequences. A parser that checks the UTF-8 form of its input but still interprets some illegal sequences as characters can be fooled. One example: a parser bans NUL when it appears as 00 but accepts the illegal C0 80 as NUL. Another: it bans 2F 2E 2E 2F ("/../") but accepts 2F C0 AE 2E 2F. The RFC says this last trick was used in a widespread virus attacking Web servers in 2001, so the threat is real.

A second risk is buffer overflow when encoding. The ISO description allows character numbers up to U+7FFFFFFF, with sequences of up to 6 bytes, so the range must be limited to U+10FFFF or buffers must allow for 5- and 6-byte sequences.

Third, the same visible text can be several distinct character sequences, such as the precomposed U+00E9 (E ACUTE) versus the sequence U+0065 U+0301 (E plus COMBINING ACUTE). That matters in string matching, for example an identifier in a credential versus an access control list entry. The RFC points to Unicode Normalization Forms as the remedy.
sections.plainLanguage: Programs must refuse byte patterns that are not valid UTF-8. If a program checks the front door but a sneaky shape of bytes slips through a side door, an attacker can bypass its checks. The same visible letter can also be written two different ways, so string comparisons should normalize first.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 2279
sections.content:
This memo obsoletes RFC 2279. It restricts the character range to U+0000 through U+10FFFF, the range reachable with UTF-16, and makes Unicode the normative source of the UTF-8 definition while ISO/IEC 10646 stays the reference for characters.

Terminology was straightened out: UTF-8 is now described as an encoding form of the character number, and UCS-2 and UCS-4 almost disappeared from the text. The warning against decoding invalid sequences became a normative MUST NOT.

New material includes the byte order mark section, the ABNF syntax, and an expanded security section covering Unicode normalization. The suggested UNICODE-1-1-UTF-8 MIME charset registration was removed.
sections.plainLanguage: This is the second edition of the UTF-8 memo. It tightens the rules, adds a grammar and a byte order mark section, and turns the safety warnings into firm requirements.
